bullet: He belonged to the Federal staff and was taken prisoner with other officers in February 1865 in one of Grant's failed raids on Richmond (I.2 ¶3). *(Drafted.)*
He is a native of Massachusetts, an engineer and a first-rate scholar to whom the Union government had given the direction of the railways during the war (I.2 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He is a true Northern American: lean, bony, gaunt, about forty-five, already greying; cropped hair, and of his beard he kept only a thick moustache (I.2 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He has one of those fine "numismatic" heads, with ardent eyes and a serious mouth, the face of a scholar of the militant school (I.2 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He wished to begin by handling hammer and pick, so he has supreme skill of hand as well as ingenuity of mind (I.2 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He is a man of action as much as a man of thought, with a tenacity that defies bad luck (I.2 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He is very learned, very practical and "très-débrouillard", and stays master of himself whatever the circumstances (I.2 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
His motto might have been William of Orange's: "Je n’ai pas besoin d’espérer pour entreprendre, ni de réussir pour persévérer." (I.2 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He is courage personified; he fought in every battle of the war, beginning in Grant's Illinois volunteers (I.2 ¶5). *(Drafted.)*
His battles include Paducah, Belmont, Pittsburg-Landing, the siege of Corinth, Port-Gibson, Black River, Chattanooga, Wilderness and the Potomac (I.2 ¶5). *(Drafted.)*
Chance always favoured him until he was wounded and taken on the battlefield of Richmond (I.2 ¶5). *(Drafted.)*
He healed quickly of his wound, and during his convalescence made the reporter's acquaintance (I.2 ¶12). *(Drafted.)*
He and Gédéon Spilett took to each other and learned to value each other, and had one aim: to escape and rejoin Grant's army (I.2 ¶12). *(Drafted.)*
He is an abolitionist "de raison et de cœur" and had long since freed Nab, born on his estate of slave parents; Nab is his devoted servant (I.2 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*
He calls Spilett his friend and Nab his servant (I.2 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
He is the most ingenious and the most learned of the five, their undisputed chief (I.5 ¶86). *(Drafted.)*
His practical science and inventive mind are what the castaways would count on in their bareness (I.6 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
His pockets are empty, except the waistcoat pocket, which holds his watch (I.8 ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
He wears shoes, which fit exactly the footprints found on the sand (I.8 ¶79). *(Drafted.)*
His will is of the most energetic (I.8 ¶83). *(Drafted.)*
He observes the country closely from the litter; its outline is engraved in his mind (I.8 ¶87). *(Drafted.)*
To his companions he is a microcosm, a compound of all human science and intelligence; with him they cannot despair (I.9 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*
Île ou continent ? is his fixed idea (I.9 ¶32). *(Drafted.)*
He makes a lens from the two watch glasses (his own and the reporter's), filled with water and sealed at the rims with a little clay, and with it lights dry moss (I.10 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
His eye is trained to judge heights and distances (I.10 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*
He has almost wholly recovered his strength by the day before the ascent (I.10 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*
He is "évidemment un esprit méthodique" (I.10 ¶16). *(Drafted.)*
He is not a man to be drawn from his fixed idea, the mountain he means to climb (I.10 ¶21). *(Drafted.)*
His confidence rests on his own power to wrest from wild nature all that is needed; his companions fear nothing because he is with them (I.11 ¶3). *(Drafted.)*
He speaks in a calm, grave voice (I.11 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
He will hide nothing of their situation from his companions (I.11 ¶43). *(Drafted.)*
He wants the principal features named for their country and its great citizens, and the rivers, gulfs and capes by their shape (I.11 ¶63). *(Drafted.)*
His watch stopped while he lay in the dunes (I.12 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He knows sulphur by its smell, and so tells the smoke from the sulphur spring from a fire of men (I.12 ¶32). *(Drafted.)*
He judges the warmth of the spring at ninety-five degrees Fahrenheit by the feel of his hand, which finds it neither warm nor cold (I.12 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*
An engineer, called "l’ingénieur Smith" in the narration (I.13 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He is addressed as "monsieur Cyrus" in the balloon's basket; the text there does not name the person addressed (I.1 ¶3). *(My reading, to confirm.)*
He could not have been better seconded than by his companions, whose aptitudes he had learned by questioning them (I.13 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He had questioned his companions about what they could do (I.13 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He is the master of the dog Top (I.13 ¶25). *(Drafted.)*
He is one of five men judged hard to match for fighting fate (I.13 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*
He is one of the Americans described as religious men who keep the Bible's precepts (I.13 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*
He knows his own height to a line, and so measures a twelve-foot pole against it (I.14 ¶7). *(Drafted.)*
He measures the granite wall by similar triangles, to avoid measuring it directly (I.14 ¶17). *(Drafted.)*
He has no chart of the Pacific, but his memory keeps a very clear picture of its southern part (I.14 ¶54). *(Drafted.)*
He finds noon without an instrument by the shortest shadow of a rod planted in the sand (I.14 ¶68). *(Drafted.)*
With only the two steel blades from Top's collar, he is so adroit, and his companions help him so intelligently, that in three days the colony has a blowing machine (I.15 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*
He means to reduce the ore by the Catalan method, simplified as it is used in Corsica (I.15 ¶41). *(Drafted.)*
He means to spare himself the furnaces and crucibles of the Catalan method, and to form with ore and coal a cubic mass at whose centre he will direct the blast of his bellows (I.15 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
He makes cementation steel by heating the pure iron with powdered charcoal in a crucible of refractory clay (I.15 ¶49). *(Drafted.)*

He knows the large snake is not venomous, being of the diamond-snake kind that the natives of New South Wales eat, and that deadly kinds may exist, the deaf viper with forked tail and the winged snake with two ear-flaps (I.16 ¶29). *(Drafted.)*
He knows alligators are found only in regions of lower latitude (I.16 ¶43). *(Drafted.)*
He is a practical man, who looks to soda rather than lime for the saponification, since lime gives insoluble, useless soaps (I.17 ¶45). *(Drafted.)*
He guides Gédéon Spilett, Harbert, Nab and Pencroff so skilfully that they become "les plus adroits ouvriers du monde" (I.17 ¶49). *(Drafted.)*
He knows that in Bohemia sulphuric acid is made by simpler means, at a higher concentration, as the acid called Nordhausen acid (I.17 ¶52). *(Drafted.)*
He knows nitro-glycerine detonates on shock, and has the idea of a suspended mass of iron, dropped by a burning fibre, to set it off (I.17 ¶71, ¶72). *(Drafted.)*
He says the nitro-glycerine could blow up the island, the continents and the earth itself, "une question de quantité" (I.18 ¶7). *(Drafted.)*

He holds nitro-glycerine too shattering to charge firearms, but says gun-cotton or ordinary powder would be easy, since they have nitric acid, saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal, and that what they lack are the arms (I.18 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*
On the descent he follows the passage's bends and keeps track of its general direction, toward the sea (I.18 ¶34). *(Drafted.)*
He estimates the depth of the well from the time a burning branch takes to fall: about ninety feet (I.18 ¶49). *(Drafted.)*
He had judged the slope and length of the passage during the descent, and so believes the cavern's seaward wall cannot be very thick (I.18 ¶58). *(Drafted.)*
He is "l’homme des grands moyens" (I.19 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*
His attachment to Harbert grows (I.19 ¶25). *(Drafted.)*
His ingenuity fails him over clothes: he has had to see to the most pressing needs first, and means to make warm, strong cloth from mouflon wool once the fine season comes (I.20 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*

He holds that an island should have a milder climate than a continent in the same latitude, because the sea is "un immense réservoir" that stores the summer's heat and gives it back in winter (I.20 ¶7, ¶9). *(Drafted.)*

He knows that heating fat with sulphuric acid frees the glycerine and leaves oleine, margarine and stearine to be parted by boiling water, and chooses instead to saponify the seal fat with lime, to simplify the work (I.20 ¶18, ¶23). *(Drafted.)*
He makes a fine pair of snuffers for the candles (I.20 ¶25). *(Drafted.)*

He knows how fast seed multiplies: a grain of wheat gives ten ears, an ear bears eighty grains on average, a poppy carries thirty-two thousand seeds and a tobacco plant three hundred and sixty thousand (I.20 ¶46, ¶48, ¶50). *(Drafted.)*
He sees at once what a single grain of wheat is worth ("Nous en ferons du pain"), and holds that in their state everything can serve (I.20 ¶41, ¶60). *(Drafted.)*

He holds that the coral infusoria are building the Pacific's new continents, and, of the two views on how the globe will end, takes the one that has it cool through the dying of its inner fires (I.21 ¶36, ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
He believes the future of the world to be "le secret de l’Auteur de toutes choses" and "le secret de Dieu" (I.21 ¶42, ¶44). *(Drafted.)*

He instructs his companions in everything, explaining chiefly the practical applications of science; he is "un livre toujours prêt, toujours ouvert à la page dont chacun avait besoin" (I.22 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*
He insists that no one risk his health, since he needs every hand (I.22 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*
He holds that without special tools it would be almost impossible to make a gun that would serve, and keeps putting the work off (I.22 ¶57). *(Drafted.)*
His chief care in the spring is clothing, not firearms; he means to raise a flock of mouflons for wool, and to found a farm (I.22 ¶59). *(Drafted.)*

He is quick to see the use of a thing and spare it: he will not let Pencroff smash the chest ("qui peut nous être utile"), and says that if survivors are found it will be given back to its owners (II.2 ¶33, ¶40). *(Drafted.)*
He plans to make an explosive substance to spare the powder (II.3 ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
He knows that eucalyptus forests neutralise marsh miasmas, and that they are called "arbres à fièvre" in Australia and New Zealand because they prevent fever (II.3 ¶48, ¶50, ¶54). *(Drafted.)*
He had made his companions promise not to fire without need, and asks them to avoid any ill-timed shot so as not to signal their presence near the coast (II.3 ¶7; II.4 ¶3). *(Drafted.)*
His plan to hide the old outlet's mouth under the lake is not yet carried out; the mouth is closed by a wall of cemented stones (II.6 ¶67). *(Drafted.)*
He has found Red Creek's flow considerable enough to feed a second ditch from the lake, whose overflow would fall by a second fall into the Mercy (II.7 ¶22). *(Drafted.)*
The ingenuity of "un homme qui s'entendait merveilleusement à ces travaux" carries the bridge over the Mercy, which took three weeks (II.7 ¶28, ¶29). *(My reading, to confirm.)*
For the ditch he has nitro-glycerine made anew, since two to three feet of soil lie over granite, and it does its accustomed work (II.7 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
He is a practical mind, who cannot think of leaving the island in a hot-air balloon over a sea without limits (II.7 ¶47). *(Drafted.)*
He has the idea of reusing the thread that sewed the strips of the balloon (II.8 ¶2). *(Drafted.)*

He has found no trace of lead on the island and substitutes iron shot, larger and lighter in effect, which is easy to make; he could make powder from saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal but judges it difficult to make good without special tools (II.8 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*

He chooses to make pyroxyle (gun-cotton), knowing that cellulose, which is nearly pure in cotton, hemp and flax fibre, paper, old linen and elder pith, is its basis; elders abound near the mouth of Red Creek (II.8 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*

He knows its faults, great unevenness of effect, excessive inflammability (it ignites at a hundred and seventy degrees against two hundred and forty) and too instantaneous a deflagration that may wear out guns; and its merits: it is not spoiled by damp, does not foul the barrel, and has four times the propellant force of ordinary powder (II.8 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*

Having sulphuric acid, he has already made nitric acid from the saltpetre nature supplies; with only ordinary nitric acid, mixed three volumes to five of concentrated sulphuric, he obtains the same result as with fuming acid (II.8 ¶10, ¶13). *(Drafted.)*

To the Oswego tea and the fermented liquor of the dragon-tree roots he adds a true beer, brewed from boiled and fermented young shoots of "abies nigra", the "spring-berr" or spruce beer (II.8 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*
He was thrown into the sea when the balloon fell (III.16 ¶62). *(Drafted.)*
The balloon carried prisoners of the Southerners (III.16 ¶62). *(Drafted.)*
Captain Nemo saved him from the sea (III.16 ¶62). *(Drafted.)*

The sight of the sand melted and vitrified by lightning on the shore leads him to believe that thick, solid panes could be made to garnish the windows against wind, rain and hail (II.9 ¶5). *(Drafted.)*
He installs a lathe, which lets him turn small toilet and kitchen utensils, and especially buttons, whose lack was keenly felt (II.9 ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
He is not a hunter (II.9 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*

He makes glass: he first has to adapt the old pottery kiln, and after several failed trials he sets up a glassworks; the shore gives sand, the lime chalk, the sea plants soda, the pyrites sulphuric acid, the soil coal for the kiln (II.9 ¶33, ¶34). *(Drafted.)*

He gathers the molten paste with the glassmaker's cane, turns it on a metal plate, has Harbert blow, and lengthens the bubble by a pendulum motion into a cylinder; the cylinder is split along its length and flattened with a wooden roller to make the first pane (II.9 ¶36, ¶39, ¶40). *(Drafted.)*
He owns the sextant found in the chest, a more perfect instrument than the one he used before (II.9 ¶70, ¶72). *(Drafted.)*
By his second observation he finds that, despite the imperfection of his instruments, he had worked so skilfully that his first error had not passed five degrees (II.9 ¶83). *(Drafted.)*
He knows maritime construction as he knows nearly everything, and seeks the model of the boat first on paper (II.10 ¶7). *(Drafted.)*
He knows the whalebone device of the Aleutian hunters of Russian America, and describes how it kills an animal that swallows the bait (II.10 ¶75). *(Drafted.)*
He is in the secret of the tobacco and prepares it (II.10 ¶33, ¶100). *(Drafted.)*

Having no carders, combers, spinners or loom, he means to use the property of wool filaments, pressed in every direction, of tangling into felt; he builds a fulling mill driven by the shore waterfall, where his quality as engineer served him well (II.11 ¶3, ¶6). *(Drafted.)*

He does not approve of the voyage to Tabor, which is only a matter of curiosity since no help can be found on that desert, half-arid rock; a journey of a hundred and fifty miles in a relatively small boat over unknown seas causes him some apprehension (II.11 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*
He calls Harbert 'cet enfant, dont le hasard a fait notre fils' (II.11 ¶23). *(Drafted.)*
He has been much involved in the affairs of the Union, and holds his listeners with accounts, views and forecasts (II.11 ¶41). *(Drafted.)*

He knows the figures of the coal workings, and foresees that coal will one day be replaced by water decomposed into hydrogen and oxygen, 'probably' by electricity; 'L’eau est le charbon de l’avenir' (II.11 ¶50, ¶63). *(Drafted.)*
He makes the pulleys on the lathe, on Pencroff's advice (II.12 ¶12). *(Drafted.)*
He gives the order that places the colonists in a line on the narrow bank between the river and the granite wall (II.12 ¶40). *(Drafted.)*

He would not hesitate, in a pressing case, to trust the Bonadventure even for a longer crossing, but would see Pencroff leave for Tabor with pain, since nothing obliges him to go (II.12 ¶110). *(Drafted.)*
He holds that isolation quickly destroys reason ("Malheur à qui est seul") and that a few months before, the man of Tabor was a man like them (II.15 ¶24). *(Drafted.)*
He believes the unknown not incurable, since despair made him what he is, and that the soul in him will be saved among his fellows (II.15 ¶32). *(Drafted.)*
He treats the unknown as a sick man and will not hurry him (II.15 ¶67). *(Drafted.)*
He decides to put the unknown to the test by moving him before the ocean and the forest edge, and does not believe he will flee (II.15 ¶70, ¶74). *(Drafted.)*

He says there is "quelque douloureux mystère" about the unknown, will respect his secrets, and holds that if he has done wrong he has cruelly atoned and is absolved in the colonists' eyes (II.16 ¶6, ¶25). *(Drafted.)*
He will not provoke the unknown to tell his story and will decide what to do only when it is told (II.16 ¶49, ¶64). *(Drafted.)*
He reasons that a man sure of deliverance at a set time would have waited and not thrown the document into the sea (II.16 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*
He is certain, "par une sorte de pressentiment", that the unknown will come back, calling the flight "la dernière révolte de cette rude nature" (II.16 ¶77, ¶78, ¶95, ¶96). *(Drafted.)*

He decides on a windmill on the heights of Grande-Vue rather than a mill at the Mercy's second fall, draws the plans, and gives the carpenters the templates to follow (II.16 ¶82, ¶85, ¶86). *(Drafted.)*

He knows the miller's rule that a mill does most work when the wings' turns a minute are six times the feet a second the wind travels, and warns Pencroff against too much wind (II.16 ¶90, ¶92). *(Drafted.)*
He makes soda at the Chimneys, with the reporter, the soap supply being used up (II.16 ¶99). *(Drafted.)*
He and Gédéon Spilett work together, now as chemists, now as physicists (II.17 ¶3). *(Drafted.)*
He understands what passes in the soul of the guilty man, and holds him back by the hand, insisting on purpose on the cordial name of "mon ami" (II.17 ¶13, ¶25). *(Drafted.)*
He pardons Ayrton after the tale ("vous avez expié vos crimes") and offers him fellowship (II.17 ¶86). *(Drafted.)*
He holds that Ayrton told the truth, since it was cruel enough for him (II.18 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*
He says he believes nothing and knows nothing, and puts the bottle among the incidents he has not been able to explain (II.18 ¶20). *(Drafted.)*

He resolves to put the corral in instant communication with Granite-house, and reckons on having every element for a battery, the hardest part being the drawing of the iron wire (II.18 ¶28, ¶33). *(Drafted.)*

He makes a drawplate, a steel plate pierced with conical holes of several gauges, tempered "de tout son dur" and fixed on a frame sunk in the ground a few feet from the great fall (II.18 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*

He draws the island's excellent iron into wire by the fulling mill's shaft, and gets lengths of forty to fifty feet that are easy to join and stretch over the five miles between the corral and Granite-house (II.18 ¶36, ¶37, ¶38). *(Drafted.)*

He makes a very simple battery, like the one Becquerel devised in 1820, using zinc only, with nitric acid and potash at hand; the potash comes from burning various plants (II.18 ¶41, ¶43). *(Drafted.)*

He makes two batteries, one for Granite-house and one for the corral, and a very simple receiver and manipulator: an electromagnet, a soft-iron plate and a needle on a dial bearing the letters of the alphabet (II.18 ¶47, ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
The telegraph is wholly installed on 12 February; posts with glass insulators were begun on 6 February (II.18 ¶46, ¶49). *(Drafted.)*
He never lets a week pass without going to see Ayrton at the corral (II.18 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*
He tells Pencroff that counting the wheat's four hundred thousand million grains at three hundred a minute would take about five thousand five hundred years (II.18 ¶52). *(Drafted.)*
He says that if the colonists leave the island it will be because they are far from "ce qu’un homme doit chérir le plus au monde, sa famille, ses amis, son pays natal" (II.19 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
He wants to see for himself the whole of his domain, and prefers to anchor near land at night so as to see the coast by day (II.19 ¶36, ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
He leaves the sailing to Pencroff (II.19 ¶65). *(Drafted.)*
He asks the reporter, a twentieth time, whether the fire might not have been a partial eruption of the volcano or some meteor (II.20 ¶34, ¶35). *(Drafted.)*
He speaks in the calm tone that is usual with him (III.1 ¶31); and gives his battle plan in "la voix la plus calme", as if it were work to direct and not a battle to settle (III.3 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*

He gives Ayrton his hand, as he is used to doing (III.1 ¶39); he understands what is passing in Ayrton's soul, and feels that a refusal would have deeply saddened the former convict (III.1 ¶88; III.2 ¶21). *(Drafted.)*
At the sight of the ship he fears rather than hopes for her coming (III.1 ¶55). *(Drafted.)*
After the brig's sinking he says "cette fois, nous saurons !", but not what, "Plus tard ! plus tard !" (III.4 ¶4, ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
He observes the wrecked hull "dans un étonnement silencieux" (III.4 ¶60). *(Drafted.)*
In the war of the Union he had occasion to try torpedoes, and so cannot mistake the work of one (III.5 ¶1). *(Drafted.)*
He knows guns: he judges the brig's four breech-loading steel cannon to be of excellent make, able to bear a heavy charge (III.5 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff has often shown great deference to his opinions (III.5 ¶67). *(Drafted.)*
He will not have the convicts hunted before they act: they may come round to other feelings and repent, and he asks that the colonists attack only if attacked (III.5 ¶56, ¶69). *(Drafted.)*
He kills a convict at the corral with his dagger, struck to the heart, after the man's ball has gone through his hat; the dagger is "plus sûr encore que son fusil" (III.7 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*

With Spilett he treats Harbert's wounds by their plain good sense, and they act as the best surgeon would have done; he and Spilett and Pencroff grow very skilful at dressing the wounded boy (III.7 ¶44; III.8 ¶10). *(Drafted.)*

He knows that men complete one another in society and are needed by one another; he wonders whether some circumstance may arise that the colonists would be powerless to overcome (III.8 ¶21). *(Drafted.)*
He thinks that he and his companions, so fortunate until now, have entered an ill-starred period, and that their luck is turning (III.8 ¶22, ¶23). *(Drafted.)*
At the sight of the devastated plateau he is paler than usual and holds down, with difficulty, an inner anger, saying not a word (III.10 ¶31). *(Drafted.)*
He holds that fires round a camp would suffice against jaguars and beasts, but would draw the convicts rather than stop them, so that darkness is better (III.11 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
He says they will find the superior being who works such wonders only if it pleases him at last to call them to himself (III.13 ¶33, ¶43). *(Drafted.)*
He sets about exploring the tangle of buttresses "avec une sévère méthode", and takes an exact survey of the mountain, carrying his search to its lowest foundations (III.13 ¶65, ¶94). *(Drafted.)*

He proposes a bigger ship than the Bonadventure, of two hundred and fifty to three hundred tons, able to carry them to the Polynesian archipelagos or New Zealand; he finds the Scottish yacht's arrival at Tabor "fort problématique" (III.14 ¶8, ¶10). *(Drafted.)*
He draws the plan of the new vessel and fixes her gauge (III.14 ¶15). *(Drafted.)*

He conceives the plan of fortifying the corral: raising the palisaded enclosure and flanking it with a sort of blockhouse; Granite-house being inexpugnable by its position, the corral would always be the pirates' objective (III.14 ¶24). *(Drafted.)*

He explains the island's hard winters: islands and coastal regions suffer less from cold than inland countries; the southern hemisphere is colder than the northern; the pack ice must be near; and the earth is farthest from the sun in the austral winter (III.14 ¶31, ¶33, ¶37, ¶39). *(Drafted.)*

From sea salt he easily extracted soda and chlorine, made the soda into carbonate of soda and the chlorine into chlorides of lime and others, used for domestic purposes and for bleaching linen (III.14 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
By the beach fall he sets up a hydraulic sawmill, worked by a wheel, two cylinders and pulleys, that saws trunks into planks and joists faster (III.15 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*

He sets out for his companions the pros and cons of an eruption, without exaggerating; Granite-house seems not menaced barring an earthquake, but the corral would have everything to fear if a new crater opened in the south walls of Mont Franklin (III.15 ¶5, ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
He understands that the despatch did not start from the corral but from the mysterious retreat, which an additional wire joins directly to Granite-house (III.15 ¶71). *(Drafted.)*
He greets the man on the divan by his name: "Capitaine Nemo, vous nous avez demandés ? Nous voici." (III.15 ¶147). *(Drafted.)*
He promises Nemo to carry out his last wishes, and by that promise binds his companions and himself (III.17 ¶20, ¶21, ¶37). *(Drafted.)*

He tells his friends it is useless to discuss submarine vessels: the Nautilus is not theirs, they have no right to dispose of it, and Nemo's wish that she be engulfed with him is formal, "et nous l’accomplirons" (III.17 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*
The plans he gave for the new ship are judged excellent: she will behave well at sea (III.18 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*
He is inclined to think the storms of the air are linked with the troubles inside the earth, since the storms come with a recrudescence of volcanic signs (III.18 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*

He weighs the coming eruption more gravely than Pencroff: the old lava road is still open and the crater has so far poured north, but an island of basalt on one side, granite on the other, lava to the north and loose soil to the south could be broken up by an earthquake (III.18 ¶24, ¶27). *(Drafted.)*

He explains the vibrations felt in the ground by the effervescence of the central fire: the earth's crust is only the wall of a boiler, which vibrates like a sounding plate under the pressure of gases (III.18 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
He reads the ash that falls on the corral, pozzolana and powdered pumice, as proof that the trouble is deep in the lower layers of the volcano (III.18 ¶65). *(Drafted.)*
He tells his companions that Lincoln Island is doomed to a destruction whose cause is in itself and that nothing can avert (III.19 ¶2, ¶3). *(Drafted.)*

He found in the crypt that the cracks in the wall closing its end were widening under the inner pressure, and that the wall would in time let in the sea, which on reaching the central chimney would blow up the island as the Mediterranean rushing into Etna would blow up Sicily (III.19 ¶13, ¶15, ¶17). *(Drafted.)*
He is used to putting figures on grave situations, and tells the truth to men he knows able to hear it, whatever it be (III.19 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
His rule, given to Pencroff when the colonists doubt the use of working at the boat: "il faut faire son devoir jusqu’au bout" (III.19 ¶45). *(Drafted.)*
He grasps at once that the lava must be dammed and made to fall into the lake, and his thought is understood by the others (III.19 ¶48, ¶49). *(Drafted.)*
On the bare rock after the island's end he is calm (III.20 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
He prays that God receive the soul of Captain Nemo, whom he calls "notre sauveur" (III.20 ¶41). *(Drafted.)*
He tells Robert Grant that where he left a culprit he finds a man "que l’expiation a refait honnête", whose hand he is proud to give (III.20 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
Fifteen days after the rescue the colonists land in America, to find their country at peace after the war (III.20 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*

Its left bank leads from the plateau down to the Chimneys (I.12 ¶74). *(Drafted.)*

In the cold of early July ice heaps up at its mouth (I.21 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
Its current is a tireless motor, used to float timber down until the cold chains it (I.21 ¶5). *(Drafted.)*

The Bonadventure’s anchor bites the sand near its mouth before she sails (II.12 ¶94). *(Drafted.)*

It has a watering place (aiguade) at its mouth, where Smith thinks the pirates might fill their casks (III.2 ¶2). *(Drafted.)*

Reefs at its mouth wreck the pirates’ second boat (III.3 ¶47). *(Drafted.)*
Its mouth is a bad place for a boat, and the sea is hard there (III.6 ¶46). *(Drafted.)*
Smith and Nab go up its left bank, and the opposite bank, in the thick wood, shows no suspect sign (III.10 ¶23). *(Drafted.)*

It is fed more directly by abundant springs lost under the cover of the Jacamar wood (III.13 ¶68). *(Drafted.)*
Excellent salmon run again up its waters (III.14 ¶20). *(Drafted.)*

Its mouth lies between the islet and the granite wall, where a ship moored would risk being crushed in a dislocation; the colonists camp under a tent near it after leaving Granite-house (III.19 ¶60, ¶68). *(Drafted.)*
The animals driven from the burning forest take refuge on the side of the Mercy (III.19 ¶60). *(Drafted.)*
A river called the Mercy is named in the colonists’ domain in Iowa (see [the Iowa domain](iowa-domain.md)) (III.20 ¶52). *(Drafted.)*
It is planned as a pen to lodge the mouflons or other wool-bearing animals that are to be captured, to answer the problem of winter clothes (II.7 ¶5, ¶6). *(Drafted.)*

It is founded at the end of January, near the sources of the Red Creek at the foot of Mont Franklin, to hold the ruminants whose presence would be a nuisance at Granite-house, especially the mouflons that are to give wool (II.8 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*

The grass is fresh, and the scattered trees let the air move freely over it (II.8 ¶32). *(Drafted.)*

Smith adds vast plank sheds under which the ruminants can shelter; all of it is built very solidly because the mouflons are robust animals whose first violence is to be feared (II.8 ¶35). *(Drafted.)*
It takes no less than three weeks to build (II.8 ¶35). *(Drafted.)*
On 7 February a drive at the foot of Mont Franklin shuts into it about thirty mouflons and a dozen wild goats, most of the mouflons females, some soon to give birth (II.8 ¶36, ¶39, ¶40). *(Drafted.)*
The prisoners tried to overthrow the palisade and failed, and soon grew quieter (II.8 ¶41). *(Drafted.)*
Under its sheds the mouflon flock grows, with several lambs bleating already (II.9 ¶17). *(Drafted.)*
The onagga, the goats and the ewes of the corral supply the colony’s daily milk (II.9 ¶63). *(Drafted.)*

Under the south-east buttress of Mont Franklin it escapes the worst of the winter gales (see [Mont Franklin](mont-franklin.md)) (II.11 ¶76). *(Drafted.)*

Smith intends to build a farm there (II.16 ¶79). *(Drafted.)*
The corral lies at the foot of the mountain, four or five miles from Granite-house, and has only stables, hardly fit for animals, at the time Ayrton asks to live there (II.17 ¶19, ¶21). *(Drafted.)*
The flock of mouflons there counts more than eighty head in December 1866 (II.17 ¶28). *(Drafted.)*

The corral is joined to Granite-house, five miles off, by a telegraph wire, so as to be in instant communication (see [the telegraph](../things/the-telegraph.md)) (II.18 ¶28, ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
One of the photographs shows the clearing and the corral backed against the first croups of the mountain (II.18 ¶61). *(Drafted.)*

In the winter it is less exposed than the plateau and covered in great part by Mont Franklin, so that it receives only the remains of the gales already broken by the forests and the high rocks of the coast; the damage there is slight (II.20 ¶78). *(Drafted.)*
Its palisade can be climbed at the angles and straddled at the top (III.7 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*
The door has an inside latch and is held shut from within by props; the house stands inside the enclosure (III.6 ¶92; III.7 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*
The part of the enclosure backed against the spur is the side from which an attack could come (III.7 ¶89). *(Drafted.)*
Its supplies can last a long time (III.8 ¶2). *(Drafted.)*
The convicts know it to be well stocked, and it holds precious resources for them (III.9 ¶12; III.10 ¶25). *(Drafted.)*
It lies among the buttresses of Mont Franklin (III.11 ¶24). *(Drafted.)*

The mouflons and goats sleep in their stables (III.12 ¶45). *(Drafted.)*
The ridge of the buttress overlooks it (III.12 ¶99). *(Drafted.)*

By moonlight it shows its clumps of trees, its small stream and its broad carpet of grass; on the mountain side the house and part of the palisade stand out white, and the gate end is dark (see [the corral stream](the-corral-stream.md), [the corral gate](the-corral-gate.md)) (III.12 ¶100). *(Drafted.)*

Many water birds frequent its banks (I.12 ¶68). *(Drafted.)*

The clearing lies two hundred paces from Lake Grant (I.13 ¶29). *(Drafted.)*

The poultry-yard lies on its south-east shore (II.7 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*
Fishing in it is fruitful (II.8 ¶15). *(Drafted.)*

Fine sand covers its floor (I.5 ¶1). *(Drafted.)*

The forge and furnaces were found nearly intact, protected by the heap of sand (I.22 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
Bows and arrows are kept in a passage of the Chimneys, where there are also a few score fathoms of light hibiscus cord (II.6 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
The canoe is hauled up on the strand next to it (II.5 ¶118). *(Drafted.)*
In the recess between the Chimneys and the wall a yard is prepared for the Bonadventure (see [the boatyard](the-boatyard.md)) (II.10 ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
A forge stands at the Chimneys, where the boat’s ironwork is made (II.12 ¶84). *(Drafted.)*
Smith and Spilett work at "l’atelier des Cheminées" (II.18 ¶16). *(Drafted.)*
Its fittings might escape the pirates’ eyes, Smith hopes (III.2 ¶2). *(Drafted.)*
From it a gun commands the strand at the foot of Granite-house over a fairly wide radius (III.3 ¶7). *(Drafted.)*
A small return of the wall hides the way from the Chimneys to the lift from the sea (III.3 ¶91). *(Drafted.)*
On 30 November the colonists are at work in its workshop (III.4 ¶82). *(Drafted.)*
Its workshops would not have escaped the devastation (III.10 ¶22). *(Drafted.)*
The ladders of the old ascent are brought there and buried deep in the sand on 15 February (III.11 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
The timber for the new ship is hauled to it and the building yard set up there (see [the boatyard](the-boatyard.md)) (III.14 ¶15). *(Drafted.)*
A great plank shed for the seasoning timber is built beside it (see [the timber shed](the-timber-shed.md)) (III.14 ¶17). *(Drafted.)*
The river mouth lies a few steps from it (I.4 ¶64). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff calls it "a house with rooms, beds and hearth" (I.8 ¶56). *(Drafted.)*
After the storm of the day before, considerable landslips had occurred and big blocks of rock lay on the strand (I.8 ¶90). *(Drafted.)*
In front of the opening the ground was deeply gullied, having suffered a violent assault of the waves (I.8 ¶91). *(Drafted.)*
The sea had entered to the bottom of the corridors and upset and destroyed everything inside (I.8 ¶94). *(Drafted.)*
Smoke is seen escaping and whirling above the rocks as Pencroff points to the angle of the cliff on the way back to the Chimneys (I.9 ¶121). *(Drafted.)*
The kitchen of the Chimneys was supplied with pottery (I.13 ¶47). *(Drafted.)*

A yard for the Bonadventure is prepared eight days after the trees are felled, in the recess between the Chimneys and the wall, and her keel lies along the sand (see [the Bonadventure](../things/bonadventure.md)) (II.10 ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
The yard for the new ship is set up at the Chimneys, where the felled trees are hauled (see [the schooner](../things/the-schooner.md)) (III.14 ¶15). *(Drafted.)*
Smith could not have placed its sheds anywhere else near Granite-house (III.14 ¶27). *(Drafted.)*
By the end of September the carcass of the schooner stands on it (III.15 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*
The colonists work at it on the strand of Granite-house, from which the volcano cannot be seen (III.18 ¶32). *(My reading, to confirm.)*

It holds spades, picks and axes, which the colonists fetch to build the dike; it is spared for some days by the lava, and would not have been had the lava reached the beach (III.19 ¶50, ¶56, ¶67). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff wants to visit Tabor, and a boat of some size is needed for the crossing (II.10 ¶1). *(Drafted.)*
The plan settled by Smith and Pencroff: thirty-five feet of keel, nine feet of beam, a draught of no more than six feet (II.10 ¶2, ¶3). *(Drafted.)*
She is to be decked her whole length, with two hatches giving into two rooms divided by a bulkhead (II.10 ¶3). *(Drafted.)*
She is rigged as a sloop, with brigantine, staysail, fortune, topsail and jib (II.10 ¶3). *(Drafted.)*
The hull is built with planks flush rather than overlapping ("à francs bords"), the frames fitted hot after the planking, on false frames (II.10 ¶3). *(Drafted.)*

She is built of fir, a wood a little "fendif" but easy to work and as good as elm in water, chosen over the elm and fir that abound on the island (see [the firs](firs.md); [the elms](elms.md)) (II.10 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
Smith and Pencroff work on her alone, as the good season is six months off (II.10 ¶5). *(Drafted.)*

The keel, thirty-five feet long, with stern-post and stem, is laid on the sand eight days after the trees are felled, in a yard prepared in the recess between the Chimneys and the wall (see [the boatyard](../places/the-boatyard.md)) (II.10 ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
Smith knows ship-building as he knows nearly everything and first sought the model on paper; Pencroff, who worked some years in a Brooklyn yard, knows the trade’s practice (II.10 ¶7). *(Drafted.)*
The false frames are fitted on the keel only after severe calculations and mature reflection (II.10 ¶7). *(Drafted.)*
Late in May she is half planked, and her lines promise a good sea boat (II.10 ¶81). *(Drafted.)*
Work stops with the great cold, about 20 June, and she is to be finished for the next spring (II.11 ¶10). *(Drafted.)*
In September she is wholly planked and ribbed inside with frames softened by steam (II.12 ¶79). *(Drafted.)*

Ceiling and deck are finished about 15 September; the seams are caulked with oakum of dry zostera driven in with a mallet, and covered with boiling tar from the forest pines (see [the zostera](zostera.md); [the pines](pines.md)) (II.12 ¶82). *(Drafted.)*

She is ballasted with heavy pieces of granite set in a bed of lime, about twelve thousand pounds, with a deck laid over and the interior divided in two rooms, with two benches serving as chests (II.12 ¶83). *(Drafted.)*
The mast foot props the bulkhead between the two rooms, which are entered by two hatches with hoods (II.12 ¶83). *(Drafted.)*
The mast is a young straight fir without knots, squared at the heel and rounded at the head (II.12 ¶84). *(Drafted.)*
The ironwork of mast, rudder and hull is roughly but solidly made at the forge of the Chimneys (see [the Chimneys](../places/the-chimneys.md)) (II.12 ¶84). *(Drafted.)*
Yards, topmast, boom, spars and oars are all done in the first week of October (II.12 ¶84). *(Drafted.)*
She is launched on 10 October, fully rigged, pushed on rollers to the shore’s edge and taken up by the rising sea (II.12 ¶87). *(Drafted.)*
She is named Bonadventure by vote, for the baptismal name of Pencroff, who is made captain by common consent (II.12 ¶87, ¶88). *(Drafted.)*
She rides well in her water-lines and should sail well on all points (II.12 ¶89). *(Drafted.)*
Running free she is satisfactorily fast; close-hauled she makes about five quarters of the wind, holds well against leeway and tacks very well, gaining in the turn (II.12 ¶95, ¶96). *(Drafted.)*
Smith says that in a pressing case one should not hesitate to trust the Bonadventure, even for a longer crossing (II.12 ¶110). *(Drafted.)*
Her home port is to be port Ballon (see [port Ballon](../places/port-ballon.md)) (II.12 ¶122). *(Drafted.)*
For the voyage to Tabor she is loaded with some bedding, utensils, arms, ammunition, a compass and provisions for about eight days (II.13 ¶19). *(Drafted.)*
She behaves perfectly, rises easily to the swell and makes rapid way (II.13 ¶26). *(Drafted.)*
By dead reckoning she has made about a hundred and twenty miles from Lincoln in thirty-six hours, three miles and a third an hour, in a weak breeze that tends to fall (II.13 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
She has held the sea marvellously well (II.14 ¶102). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff says she is a good boat, which behaved admirably in the gale at the return (II.15 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*
At the mouth of the Mercy she is aground on the sand half the time, which tires her, and the mouth offers no shelter from the seas in east winds (II.15 ¶50, ¶52). *(Drafted.)*
On 20 October she is taken to port Ballon, round cape Griffe, and lies two hours later in its quiet waters (see [port Ballon](../places/port-ballon.md)) (II.15 ¶60). *(Drafted.)*
She is provisioned at port Ballon for a voyage that may last some time, and leaves it on 16 April (II.19 ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
She can reef: Pencroff proposes to run on at a slow speed with two reefs in her sail (II.19 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
She is well ballasted, would not have capsized, and has hatches (panneaux) that withstand the water falling aboard in the gale; Pencroff has great confidence in her (II.20 ¶2). *(Drafted.)*
In the gale Pencroff sets his jib on the main mast as a storm staysail and waits, head to land (II.20 ¶1). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff values the immersed part of her hull, her "œuvres vives", more than his own skin (II.19 ¶66, ¶67). *(Drafted.)*
A boat that Pencroff defies the pirates to find is sheltered in Port Ballon, read as the Bonadventure (III.1 ¶81). *(My reading, to confirm.)*
Beside a ship of three to four hundred tons she is small, Pencroff says, "notre Bonadventure" (III.4 ¶24). *(Drafted.)*
It lies quietly at anchor in the narrow creek of Port-Ballon, a boat of small tonnage by Pencroff’s reckoning (III.6 ¶18, ¶37). *(Drafted.)*

The convicts found her in her little port and put to sea in her; with Bob Harvey no longer there to handle her, they ran onto the rocks and she was entirely broken up, about eight days before 20 February (III.13 ¶55, ¶57). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff, who was proud of her, is dismayed at her loss (III.13 ¶63). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff says a boat of thirty to forty tons needs five to six months at least to build (III.13 ¶60). *(Drafted.)*
He tells his companions of the plan on 10 January: it is an electric telegraph (II.18 ¶29, ¶31, ¶32, ¶33). *(Drafted.)*

He means to make the battery from what they have, and to draw iron wire through a draw-plate (see [the battery](the-telegraph-battery.md); [the draw-plate](the-draw-plate.md)) (II.18 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
The wire is made first, since if it failed the battery and other accessories would be useless (see [the telegraph wire](telegraph-wire.md)) (II.18 ¶35). *(Drafted.)*
The wire, in lengths of forty to fifty feet easy to join and stretch, has to cover the five miles that separate the corral from the enclosure of Granite-house (II.18 ¶38). *(Drafted.)*

The posts, fitted with glass insulators to carry the wire, begin to be planted on 6 February along the corral road, and a few days later the wire is stretched (see [the telegraph posts](telegraph-posts.md); [the glass insulators](glass-insulators.md)) (II.18 ¶46). *(Drafted.)*
The current, the text says, travels at a hundred thousand kilometres a second, and the earth carries it back to its starting point (II.18 ¶46). *(Drafted.)*
Two batteries are made, one for Granite-house and one for the corral, so that each station can speak to the other (II.18 ¶47). *(Drafted.)*

The receiver and the manipulator are very simple: at both stations the wire winds round an electromagnet of soft iron, which magnetises while the current passes and demagnetises when it is broken; a soft-iron plate before it is drawn and released, and to this movement Smith attaches a needle on a dial carrying the letters of the alphabet (see [the telegraph instruments](telegraph-instruments.md)) (II.18 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
The whole is completely installed on 12 February, and Smith’s first call to the corral is answered satisfactorily by Ayrton (II.18 ¶49). *(Drafted.)*
Its two advantages are that it lets the colonists verify Ayrton’s presence at the corral and that it does not leave him in complete isolation (II.18 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*
It puts the corral and Granite-house in communication, and a call sent from the great hall is answered by Ayrton from the corral (III.1 ¶17, ¶20). *(Drafted.)*
If anything happens at the corral, Ayrton is to warn the colonists at once by a telegram addressed to Granite-house (III.6 ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
Ayrton acknowledges every telegram as a rule (III.6 ¶54). *(Drafted.)*
The wire between the corral and Granite-house is re-established and works when a colonist at the corral finds it necessary to spend the night there (III.14 ¶21). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff, delighted, sends a telegram to the corral every morning and every evening, and it never goes without an answer (II.18 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*

At both stations the wire winds round an electromagnet of soft iron; a soft-iron plate before it is drawn while the current passes and falls back when it stops, and Smith links to the plate a needle on a dial lettered with the alphabet (II.18 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
Granite-house has an electric bell, which announces Ayrton’s replies and falls silent when the line is cut (III.6 ¶7, ¶57). *(Drafted.)*
Granite-house has an electric bell in the hall, which rings with a vibrating hammer when a call comes (III.15 ¶23, ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
A needle moving on the alphabetical dial gives the reply to Granite-house (III.15 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*
At the corral the receiving and transmitting apparatus stands on the table with the battery, all in place (III.15 ¶63). *(Drafted.)*

Smith draws the iron, first prepared in long thin rods, through the draw-plate, and gets wire forty to fifty feet long, easy to join and stretch over the five miles between the corral and Granite-house (II.18 ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
The drawing takes only a few days, his companions turning wire-drawers once the machine is going (II.18 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
The wire is stretched a few days after the posts are planted from 6 February (II.18 ¶46). *(Drafted.)*
On 11 November it hangs evenly along the road for about two miles, then less tight (III.6 ¶75). *(Drafted.)*
In the part of the corral between the house and the palisaded enclosure there is no telegraph line (III.15 ¶74). *(Drafted.)*
They are planted from 6 February, fitted with glass insulators, to carry the wire along the road to the corral (II.18 ¶46). *(Drafted.)*
They are numbered; pole no. 74 stands half-way between Granite-house and the corral (III.6 ¶75, ¶85). *(Drafted.)*
On 11 November the posts are in good order and the insulators intact up to pole no. 74 (III.6 ¶75). *(Drafted.)*
The first post stands just beyond the gate of the corral enclosure, and carries the insulator from which the new wire hangs (see [the new wire](the-new-wire.md)) (III.15 ¶74). *(Drafted.)*
